results.summary: The design implements an asynchronous FIFO that buffers data between two clock domains with independent read and write clocks. It uses Gray-coded pointers and synchronization logic to prevent metastability, with full and empty flags indicating when the FIFO cannot accept or provide data. The documentation describes how to test by setting write and read enables and observing the flags and data outputs, but the pin list provided in the documentation does not match the actual pin names given in the project metadata. External hardware is minimal, likely just a way to drive the inputs and observe the outputs.

This project computes a dot product between a binary vector A and a ternary vector B, with ternary weights and 1-bit activations, targeting on-chip neural network inference. The inputs are eight binary elements of A and serial ternary elements of B, and the dot product result is provided on eight output pins. Testing is done via the Commander app to set inputs and weights, with no additional hardware required. The documentation is very brief, only stating the basic function and test method.

This design implements a ring oscillator operating in the GHz range, followed by a divider to produce a lower-frequency output in the 20 MHz range. It includes test and debug modes to verify divider functionality at low frequencies, and can be disabled via an enable signal. Testing requires an oscilloscope, power supply, and function generator, as described in the documentation. Silicon verification results are not provided.

This design generates an Archimedean spiral pattern for VGA display, with adjustable foreground/background colors and animation speed via input pins. It requires an external PMOD VGA adapter and optionally switches for control. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a short description and basic testing instructions.

The project implements a monophonic keyboard synthesizer with one octave of notes, generating sine waves using an efficient delta-step method. The 8-bit output is provided directly and also via a PWM generator for audio output, intended for use with Mike Bell's audio PMOD. Testing involves attaching the input PMOD to a row of buttons for playing notes. No silicon test results are mentioned.

This design is a PWM generator with configurable period (12-bit) and duty cycle (7-bit, 1%-99% coverage). It contains two 12-bit registers for duty and period, selected via a sel signal and written when wr_en is high. Testing involves connecting the output to an oscilloscope to verify frequency and duty cycle. External hardware includes a microcontroller or pattern generator to set the inputs.

This design implements a hash table with eight slots, 4-bit keys, and 4-bit values, supporting lookup, insert, and delete operations. Commands are issued via CMD and GO signals, with status and output value provided on output pins. The table handles collisions using linear probing and buffers inputs during operation. Testing involves setting keys, values, and commands, then observing status and output. No external hardware is required beyond input switches and output displays.

Wildcat is a 3-stage RISC-V CPU implementation written in Chisel. The documentation is extremely sparse, with only a one-line description and a 'TBD' for testing, and the pin names are generic. It may require external flash and RAM PMODs for operation according to the pin description. No further details on functionality, testing, or silicon results are provided.

This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It uses AND gates and full adders arranged in a grid, as described in the documentation. Testing involves applying two 4-bit inputs and reading the 8-bit product. The design is educational, likely from a class (ECE 2204), and requires no external hardware.

Warp is a demoscene demo that generates audio and video output, intended for use with VGA and audio PMODs. It can be simulated on an ECPIX5 FPGA with appropriate PMODs, and the audio also runs on an ULX3S. The documentation is minimal and uncertain, with statements like 'Maybe it works?'. External hardware includes VGA and audio PMODs, and the design is written in Silice.
